chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
title: Experimenting with Earl Hines and the Down Beat criticism
summary: He tried high and daring things at the Grand Terrace, and a Down Beat review calling him atrocious sent him practicing eight hours a day.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: And when I first started -- when I first went with Earl a lot of people thought I was nuts, some of the things I was playing because guys just weren't playing those kind of things at that particular time, you know. But to me it was a challenge to play. I figured the trumpets and all were playing like that. Why couldn't the trombones play like that way back there then.

So, it was just a different thing altogether. And trombone players didn't play real high anything like that back at that time, and I loved to play high. You know, I was just getting into it. I made a lot of bad notes trying to do it because I remember once, Stanley Dance's wife now --

And Benny Goodman was in -- Benny Goodman was in Chicago playing at the Congress Hotel. He's just getting started too. And I was with Earl Hines over at the Grand Terrace. And I'd take all kind of chances. I tried anything

I thought of -- I just tried. And naturally, it all ain't going to come out. So, I guess she came there one of those nights when it wasn't working, and she -- she wrote an article in Downbeat and said the trombone player was atrocious. And she probably was right, you know. I had to laugh about that thing, but it hurt me so bad at that time until I think I started practicing about eight hours a day after she wrote that.

I really went to practicing then. I said I'm not going to let this chick write like -- about me like that. And I just really. So, Earl and Stanley, they kid Helen when they want to kid her now. They say oh don't say nothing. You're the one that put Trummy down (unintelligible). And we were laughing about that a few days ago out there at Colorado, you know.

I said, well, Helen, you were right. I was kind of bad because I was just experimenting. And it happens to a guy who's taking chances. It's going to happen to you. It's like a ball player, you know. The guys who make the most errors are the guys who take the greatest chances. You're going to make errors if you take chances. But I was that kind. I was a gambler, you know, with that horn. I just took chances.
Some things I know I had no business trying. But -- because my technique wasn't up to what my ideas were at that particular time. But it just made me work harder to try to get
enough technique to do those things that I was attempting to do back there then.
